title: Accuracy and precision in measurement
competency: Distinguish between accuracy and precision in measurements.

keywords.def: How close a measurement is to its accepted or known value.
How close two or more measurements are to each other.

en.text: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true or known value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. You can be precise but not accurate, like darts grouped together far from the bullseye.

am.text: ትክክለኛነት ልኬቱ ለእውነተኛው ዋጋ ምን ያህል ቅርብ እንደሆነ ነው። ተቀራራቢነት ተደጋጋሚ ልኬቶች እርስ በርሳቸው ምን ያህል እንደሚቀራረቡ ነው።

screens.title: Darts
screens.ask: Four darts land close together, but far from the bullseye. How would you describe the throws?
screens.after: They agree with each other (precise) but miss the target (not accurate).

screens.title: Figure 1.8: three dartboards
items: All darts in the bullseye, close together: accurate and precise.
Darts close together but away from the bullseye: precise but not accurate.
Darts far apart and away from the bullseye: neither precise nor accurate.

screens.title: Accuracy and precision
paras: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to its accepted or known value.
Precision is how close two or more measurements are to each other.
Precision does not depend on accuracy.

screens.title: Example 1.8 on a number line

points.label: readings
points.info: Five readings: 3.1, 3.2, 3.25, 3.3 and 3.2 kg. They sit close together: precise.

points.label: true 10 kg
points.info: The known mass. The readings are about 7 kg away from it: not accurate.

screens.ask: Tap each point. Are the readings close to each other? Are they close to the true value?

screens.title: Key words
defs: How close a measurement is to its accepted or known value.
How close two or more measurements are to each other.

screens.title: Examples 1.7 and 1.8
steps: A substance's known mass is 10 kg. You measure 8.2 kg.
8.2 kg is not close to 10 kg, so the measurement is not accurate.
The values are close to each other, so they are precise.
But they are far from 10 kg, so they are not accurate.

screens.text: Accuracy and precision (Example 1.8): the known mass is 10 kg. Five readings are 3.2, 3.1, 3.25, 3.3 and 3.2 kg. They are
screens.why:
First compare the readings with each other.
They are all between 3.1 and 3.3 kg: close together, so precise.
Now compare them with the known value, 10 kg.
They are about 7 kg too low, so not accurate.
So they are precise but not accurate.
screens.clue: Compare the readings with each other, then with 10 kg.

screens.text: Accuracy and precision: g on Earth is 9.81 m/s². Students get 12.2, 12.3, 12.1 and 12.08 m/s². The results are
screens.why:
Compare the results with each other.
They are all between 12.08 and 12.3: close together, so precise.
Compare them with the true value, 9.81.
They are more than 2 m/s² too high, so not accurate.
So they are precise but not accurate.

screens.text: Accuracy and precision, true or false: a measurement can be accurate but not precise.
screens.why:
Accurate means close to the true value.
Precise means the readings agree with each other.
Readings can be scattered (not precise) all around the true value.
Their average is then close to the true value (accurate).
So it is true.

screens.title: Four kinds of results
screens.text: Accuracy and precision: the true mass is 10 kg. Sort each set of readings.
items: Close together and close to 10 kg.
Close together, but about 3 kg too low.
Spread out, but the average is 40 ÷ 4 = 10 kg.
Spread out, and the average (about 7.7 kg) is far from 10 kg.
screens.why:
First ask: are the readings close to each other? That is precision.
Then ask: are they (or their average) close to 10 kg? That is accuracy.
9.9, 10.0, 10.1: both.
7.1, 7.0, 7.2: precise only.
8, 12, 9, 11: average 10, so accurate only.
3, 6, 14: neither.
screens.clue: Check the spread first, then the average.

screens.text: Accuracy or precision? Sort each description.
items: Accuracy compares with the true value.
Precision compares readings with each other.
The bullseye is the true value.
Grouped darts agree with each other.
screens.why:
Accuracy compares a measurement with the true value.
So "close to the known value" and "hitting the bullseye" are accuracy.
Precision compares readings with each other.
So "repeated readings agree" and "darts grouped together" are precision.
screens.clue: Does it compare with the true value, or with other readings?

screens.text: Accuracy and precision: a kitchen scale always reads 50 g too much, but it gives the same reading every time. Its readings are
screens.why:
Same reading every time: the readings agree, so they are precise.
Always 50 g too much: they miss the true value, so they are not accurate.
So they are precise but not accurate.
Resetting the scale to zero would make it accurate too.
screens.clue: Do the readings agree? Are they correct?

items.text: Key words review: which is the definition of a derived quantity?
opts: It depends on one or more fundamental quantities
It cannot be expressed by other quantities
It is measured with the body
items.ans: It depends on one or more fundamental quantities
items.why:
Derived means "built from".
A derived quantity is built from fundamental quantities, like area = length × width.
A quantity that cannot be expressed by others is fundamental.
So: it depends on one or more fundamental quantities.

items.text: Indigenous measurement: which of these are indigenous methods used in Addis Ababa?
items.why:
Indigenous methods are local and traditional.
Cubit (length) uses the arm.
Quntal (mass) is a bag for grain.
Jog (volume) is a plastic cup; a tree's shadow tells the time.
Kilogram and metre are SI units, not indigenous.

items.text: Key words review: what are prefixes?
opts: A short way of writing very large or very small numbers
items.ans: A short way of writing very large or very small numbers
items.why:
Science uses very large and very small numbers.
A prefix is a short way to write them in a unit.
Example: kilo means 1000, so 5000 m = 5 km.
Instruments, indigenous units and derived quantities are other ideas.

items.text: Key words review: what is the difference between accuracy and precision?
opts: Accuracy is closeness to the known value; precision is closeness of readings to each other
Precision is closeness to the known value
items.ans: Accuracy is closeness to the known value; precision is closeness of readings to each other
items.why:
Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the known value.
Precision: how close repeated readings are to each other.
They are not the same: one is about the target, one about agreement.
So the first option is right.
items.clue: One is about the target, one about agreement.

opts: closeness of readings to each other
test.why:
Accuracy compares a measurement with the true (known) value.
The closer it is, the more accurate.
Closeness of readings to each other is precision.
So accuracy means closeness to the known value.

opts: closeness of readings to each other
test.ans: closeness of readings to each other
test.why:
Precision compares repeated readings with each other.
If they agree closely, they are precise.
Closeness to the known value is accuracy.
So precision means closeness of readings to each other.

test.text: Accuracy and precision: the known value is 5.0 g. Readings are 4.9, 5.1 and 5.0 g. These are
test.why:
Compare with each other: 4.9 to 5.1, a spread of only 0.2 g. Precise.
Compare with 5.0 g: each is within 0.1 g. Accurate.
So they are accurate and precise.

test.text: Accuracy and precision: the known value is 20 cm. Readings are 15, 25, 18 and 22 cm (average 20 cm). These are
opts: accurate on average but not precise
test.ans: accurate on average but not precise
test.why:
Compare with each other: from 15 to 25 cm, a 10 cm spread. Not precise.
Average: (15 + 25 + 18 + 22) ÷ 4 = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 cm.
The average equals the known value: accurate on average.
So they are accurate on average but not precise.

test.text: Accuracy and precision, true or false: you can be very precise but inaccurate.
test.why:
Precise: your readings agree with each other.
Inaccurate: they are far from the true value.
Example: a scale that always reads 50 g too much.
Its readings agree but are wrong. So it is true.

notes.text: Example 1.8 says "the above example 1.4" but means Example 1.7 (the 10 kg substance).
Exercise 1.9 lists 4 options for 3 dartboards; option (a) "accurate but not precise" matches none of them.
